entry: [[Nomad|Nomadic]] people of Central Asia, the Caucasus and Eastern Europe, active from the 4th to 6th centuries. They reached the [[Volga]] River by 370, prompting the westward movement of the [[Goths]] and Alans. By 430 they had established a vast but short-lived empire on the Danubian frontier of the Roman Empire. Under King [[Attila]] they raided the Eastern Roman Empire, invaded Gaul in 451, where they fought a combined army of Romans and Visigoths at the Battle of the Catalaunian Fields, and invaded Italy in 452. After Attila died in 453 they lost much of their empire at the Battle of Nedao (c. 454). Very little is known of Hunnic culture; their main method of warfare was mounted archery. The Huns may have initiated the Great Migration. A medieval legend in Hungary claimed descent from them, a link that mainstream scholarship has dismissed.

[[Manga|Japanese manga]] series written and illustrated by Yoshihiro Togashi. Serialized in *Weekly Shōnen Jump* since March 1998, with frequent hiatuses. Gon Freecss leaves home to become a licensed Hunter and find the father who left him when young. A 62-episode [[Anime|anime]] adaptation aired from 1999 to 2001, and a 148-episode version from 2011 to 2014. It is one of the best-selling manga series of all time, with over 100 million copies in circulation worldwide by June 2026.

American journalist and author, a pioneer of New Journalism. He rose to prominence with *Hell's Angels* (1967), based on a year spent with the [[Hells Angels]] motorcycle club. His 1970 article "The Kentucky Derby Is Decadent and Depraved" helped establish Gonzo, a style in which the writer becomes a participant in the narrative. *Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas* (1972), first serialized in [[Rolling Stone]], reflected on the failure of the 1960s counterculture. He was an outspoken critic of [[Richard Nixon]] and covered George McGovern's 1972 campaign for the magazine. From the mid-1970s his output declined as he struggled with fame and substance abuse. He later wrote for [[Playboy]], *Esquire* and ESPN.com until the end of his life.

Person living in a community that obtains most or all of its food from wild plants and animals. Foraging and hunting were common among most prehistoric societies, before agriculture arose in the [[Neolithic]] period. Groups usually numbered a few dozen people and were fully or semi-nomadic. The practice began with *Homo erectus* about 1.8 million years ago and occupied at least 90 percent of human history. Societies were generally egalitarian, emphasizing sharing and resisting hierarchy, and men and women often both hunted and gathered. After the [[Neolithic Revolution]], more productive farming and herding communities displaced most foragers. Today a few groups, including the San and the [[Sentinelese]], continue aspects of this lifestyle.

Fatal inherited neurodegenerative disorder. It typically presents with progressive psychiatric, cognitive and motor symptoms, including involuntary "dance-like" movements called chorea. It is usually inherited from an affected parent through a mutation in the huntingtin gene, where an expansion of CAG repeats produces a mutant protein that gradually damages the [[Basal ganglia|basal ganglia]] and other brain cells. Symptoms usually appear around the age of 40. No cure is known, and tetrabenazine can treat movement problems. Death typically occurs 15–20 years after the disease is first detected, often from complications such as pneumonia.

Family of spiders (*Sparassidae*) with more than a thousand species. Huntsman spiders catch prey by hunting rather than in webs, and are also called giant crab spiders. Many grow large; in Laos the giant huntsman (*Heteropoda maxima*) has a leg span of 25–30 cm. Their legs are twisted so that they extend forward in a crab-like fashion, and they are often confused with tarantulas. Huntsman venom is significantly less dangerous to humans than that of the [[Brown recluse spider|brown recluse]], which they are sometimes mistaken for. The wheel spider (*Carparachne aureoflava*) of the Namib uses a cartwheeling motion to move.

Most populous city in Alabama, and county seat of Madison County. It had 215,006 residents at the 2020 census and an estimated 233,627 by July 1, 2025. Founded in 1805 within the Mississippi Territory, it was designated Alabama's first capital for a year after statehood in 1819. Major growth followed World War II, when rocket research at Redstone Arsenal, established by the U.S. Army during the war, led to space exploration. [[NASA]]'s Marshall Space Flight Center is located at the arsenal, which also hosts the United States Space Command.

Track and field discipline of racing over obstacles called hurdles, a form of [[Sport of athletics|athletics]]. Hurdles are set at precisely measured heights and distances, and athletes must clear each one; passing under a hurdle or deliberately knocking it over is disqualifying. Accidental knockdowns are not penalized, as the hurdles are weighted to make them costly. The most prominent events are the 110 m for men, 100 m for women and 400 m for both sexes, all contested at the Summer Olympics. Indoor races are usually 60 m over five hurdles. Track hurdles are normally 68–107 cm high, depending on the age and sex of the hurdler. An L-shaped hurdle that tips down when struck was developed in 1935.

Atlantic hurricane of 2005, peaking at Category 5. It was the costliest tropical cyclone in the United States, with damage estimated at $125 billion. Eighty percent of [[New Orleans]] flooded after [[Levee|levees]] failed, and investigators concluded that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers was responsible for the breached floodwalls. Katrina killed 1,392 people, the deadliest American hurricane since 1928. The response led to the resignation of Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) director Michael D. Brown. The World Meteorological Organization retired the name in April 2006.

Alid political and religious leader and grandson of the Prophet [[Muhammad]]. Second son of [[Ali]] and Fatima, he is regarded in [[Shia Islam]] as the third Imam, after his brother Hasan. After Mu'awiya I died, Yazid demanded Husayn's allegiance; he refused and left [[Medina]] for [[Mecca]]. Invited by the people of Kufa, he set out with a small party, but was intercepted by an army of the caliph and killed at the Battle of Karbala. The battle became a defining event in Shia history, and both Sunni and Shia Muslims regard Husayn and his companions as martyrs. Shia Muslims mourn him each year during Muharram, culminating on Ashura.

Male spouse in a [[Marriage|marriage]]. The word derives from Middle English *huseband*, from Old English *hūsbōnda*, meaning householder. Traditionally the husband was head of the household and primary provider, a role often considered paternalistic, though he is no longer automatically the sole breadwinner. The term applies only while the marriage lasts; after divorce a man may be called an ex-husband, and after his spouse dies he is a widower. In many countries heterosexual [[Monogamy|monogamy]] is the prevailing norm, and many legal systems prohibit polygamy. In premodern unions a husband was obliged to protect and support his wife, children and household servants. Before marriage a dowry or bride price was sometimes exchanged, and the husband had to return the dowry after grave offenses against his wife.

Series of 15th-century religious wars in [[Bohemia]], fought from 1419 to approximately 1434. They began after the [[Catholic Church]] executed the reformer [[Jan Hus]] for heresy in 1415. Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund and the papacy launched several crusades against the Hussites, but the Hussites repelled them under the command of [[Jan Žižka]], using fortified wagons and early handheld firearms such as hand cannons. In 1432 the moderate Utraquists switched sides to fight alongside Catholic forces against the radical Taborites. The wars ended in 1434 with the Utraquists victorious, and the Hussites submitted to the king of Bohemia and the Roman Catholic Church, keeping their variant rite.

Small dwelling built from local materials such as mud or wood. Huts are a form of vernacular architecture, less complex to build than a house but more substantial than a [[Tent|tent]]. They are used as dwellings, for storage, workshops and teaching. Shepherds' huts have served as mobile homes for the last few hundred years, and in some indigenous societies huts are permanent homes. Climbers and backpackers use the term for solid mountain refuges, from simple bothies to larger huts with restaurants. Examples include the bahay kubo, a lightweight bamboo stilt house of the Philippines, and the [[Igloo|igloo]], a hut of hard snow or ice. In English the word was first used as a military term in the 1650s.

Nearest open star cluster to the Sun, in the constellation [[Taurus (constellation)|Taurus]]. Its distance of about 153 light-years (47 parsecs) was measured directly by parallax using the Hipparcos satellite and the [[Hubble Space Telescope]], making it an important rung on the [[Cosmic distance ladder|cosmic distance ladder]]. The cluster's hundreds of stars share the same age, origin and motion, and it is estimated to be about 625 million years old. Its brightest stars form a V shape, but [[Aldebaran]] is much closer, at 65 light-years, and is not a member. Epsilon Tauri has a gas giant exoplanet candidate, the first planet found in any open cluster.

Offspring of two organisms from different varieties, subspecies, species or genera. Each cell contains genetic material from both parents, unlike a chimera, in which cells come from different organisms. Hybrids are not always intermediate between their parents; they can show hybrid vigor, growing larger or taller than either. Roughly 25% of plants and 10% of animals form hybrids with at least one other species. Hybridization is fundamental to plant evolution, and crop [[Wheat|wheat]] arose through hybrid speciation with its number of chromosomes doubled. Human-mediated crosses of wild and domesticated species include beefalo and wolfdogs, while [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]] and modern humans are thought to have interbred as recently as 40,000 years ago.

Indian soldier and sultan of Mysore, de facto ruler from 1761. He rose to commander-in-chief under the Wodeyar rajas, came to dominate the titular monarch Krishnaraja Wodeyar II, and then governed as Chief Minister. He was the primary military leader against the [[East India Company]] in the first and second Anglo-Mysore wars. He allied with the French, who helped raise his artillery and arsenal. His rule was marked by frequent warfare with neighbors and by rebellion within his territories. He was known to [[Benjamin Franklin]] for his bravery. He left his eldest son, [[Tipu Sultan]], a kingdom bordered by the Krishna River and the Arabian Sea.

Capital and largest city of the Indian state of [[Telangana]]. Located on the Deccan Plateau along the Musi River, it had 6.9 million residents within city limits at the 2011 census and 9.7 million in its metropolitan region. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded it in 1591, and the [[Mughal Empire|Mughals]] annexed it in 1687. As imperial capital of the Asaf Jahi Nizams from 1769 to 1948, it was the center of a distinctive culture. Until the 19th century it was known as the "City of Pearls" for its pearl industry. Since the 1990s it has become a hub of pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and information technology, with the HITEC City special economic zone attracting multinationals. [[UNESCO]] lists its cuisine as a creative city of gastronomy.

Second-largest city in [[Sindh]], Pakistan, after [[Karachi]]. Founded in 1768 by Mian Ghulam Shah Kalhoro of the Kalhora dynasty on a ridge above the [[Indus River]], it was named in honor of [[Ali]], the fourth caliph, and its name means "Lion City." It served as a provincial capital until the British moved the capital to Bombay Presidency in 1840. The Talpur ruler Mir Fateh Ali Khan made it his capital in 1789, after floods in Khudabad, the previous capital. The city lies about 150 km inland of Karachi and is connected to it by rail and the M-9 motorway.

Colorless, flammable inorganic liquid with an [[Ammonia|ammonia]]-like odor, N₂H₄. It is highly hazardous unless handled in solution, such as hydrazine hydrate. Its largest use is as a precursor to blowing agents for polymer foams, and it is also used to make pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. Hydrazine is a long-term storable propellant for spacecraft and an oxygen scavenger in power plant steam cycles, where it reduces corrosion. Approximately 120,000 tons of hydrazine hydrate were manufactured worldwide per year as of 2000.

Organic compound consisting entirely of hydrogen and carbon. Hydrocarbons are generally colorless and hydrophobic, and occur as gases such as [[Methane|methane]] and propane, liquids such as hexane and benzene, low-melting solids such as paraffin wax, or polymers such as polyethylene. Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single bonds and include [[Alkane|alkanes]], while [[Alkene|alkenes]] and [[Alkyne|alkynes]] contain double or triple bonds, and aromatic hydrocarbons contain at least one aromatic ring. In the fossil fuel industries the term refers to petroleum, natural gas and coal. Combustion of hydrocarbons supplies most of the world's energy, and [[Petroleum]] is the dominant raw material for commodity chemicals such as solvents and polymers. Most human-generated greenhouse gas emissions are carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels or methane from natural gas handling and agriculture.

Aqueous solution of hydrogen chloride (HCl), a strong acid also called muriatic acid. A colorless solution with a distinctive pungent smell, it is a component of the gastric acid in the digestive systems of most animals, including humans. It is an important laboratory reagent and industrial chemical. Alchemists called it spirits of salt, and the name hydrochloric acid was coined by French chemist [[Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac]] in 1814. The Persian physician [[Abu Bakr al-Razi]] produced hydrogen chloride gas in the early tenth century, but the acid itself was isolated only later. A mixture of [[Nitric acid|nitric acid]] and hydrochloric acid, known as [[Aqua regia]], dissolves gold.

Semi-synthetic [[Opioid|opioid]] used to treat pain and as a cough suppressant. Usually taken by mouth, it is combined with acetaminophen or [[Ibuprofen|ibuprofen]] for severe pain. Common side effects include dizziness, sleepiness, nausea and constipation, while serious ones include respiratory depression and serotonin syndrome. Derived from [[Codeine|codeine]] or thebaine, it was patented in 1923. It is a Schedule II controlled substance in the United States, which consumed 99% of the worldwide supply as of 2010.

Electricity generated from hydropower, including stations with a [[Dam|dam]] and reservoir. Hydropower supplies 15% of the world's electricity, almost 4,210 TWh in 2023, more than all other renewable sources combined and more than nuclear power. It can provide large amounts of low-carbon electricity on demand, and a station with a [[Reservoir|reservoir]] can raise or lower output within seconds or minutes. Once built, it produces no direct waste and almost always emits considerably less [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]] than fossil fuel plants, although flooding lowland rainforest can release substantial amounts. Construction can displace populations, destroy arable land and disrupt river ecosystems. China added 24 GW in 2022, nearly three-quarters of global hydropower capacity additions.

Clear, very corrosive solution of [[Hydrogen fluoride|hydrogen fluoride]] in water. Typically sold as a 49% solution, it is used in laboratories to make organofluorine compounds and in industry to produce inorganic fluorides such as cryolite and aluminium trifluoride, used in [[Aluminium|aluminium]] smelting. Because it breaks down silica and most metal oxides, it is used for glass etching, for etching silicon wafers in the [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] industry, and for cleaning industrial boilers. Dilute solutions behave as a weak acid, but it may be deadly if ingested, inhaled or absorbed through the skin. Its burns can be painless at first but still need immediate attention. The acid was first prepared in 1771 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele.

Intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to an [[Electronegativity|electronegative]] donor and a lone pair on an acceptor atom. Its partial covalent character means it cannot be described as purely electrostatic, though electrostatics, charge transfer and dispersion all contribute. Typical donors and acceptors are nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine. Strength ranges from 4.2 to 167.4 kJ/mol (1 to 40 kcal/mol), stronger than van der Waals interactions but weaker than covalent or ionic bonds. Hydrogen bonding gives [[Water|water]] its unusually high boiling point and stabilizes protein and nucleic acid structures. It is also central to DNA base pairing and occurs in [[Ice|ice]].
